prize_parts.citation: for a visionary prose of great formal ambition, rooted in a poetic imagination, that builds from memory, the body and dream a cosmos of its own across decades of work

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from Adonis (B027) to Cărtărescu (B029). The reason is the test I set for myself in round 1, not the number of colleagues who prefer a candidate. I wrote that the case for Adonis has to rest on the poems, that I could not show the later collections sustain the early and middle work, and that if the committee could not establish this, a candidate whose strength is more accessible in translation would be the sounder choice. The exchange has not established it. Nobody, myself included, has offered evidence from the later poems, and the Academy's Arabic-poetry expert input is outside what this stage can supply. I would not let translation uncertainty decide the matter on its own, since that would favour writers who translate most readily. But a whole-oeuvre judgment for the final vote needs a case I can argue to colleagues from the work, and I cannot yet do that for Adonis's later output. Cărtărescu's case can be argued from structure. Public knowledge of Blinding and Solenoid points to a voice found nowhere else in this writer's work, a densely patterned prose that treats memory, the body and dream as one project, and an architecture that extends across volumes. The poetic base gives that prose its rhythm and its imaginative logic. Mattson and Sem-Sandberg both anchor the case in the prose project and treat the poetry as foundation, and I accept that scope. Whether the late volumes deepen or repeat the earlier ones remains open. That uncertainty applies to every candidate on this shortlist, and the architectural scale at least gives it something concrete to be tested against. In answer to the chair's question on my own alternatives, Carson and Cărtărescu were close to equal in my opening ranking. I now place Cărtărescu first on a narrow judgment about cumulative formal achievement, and I keep Carson as a strong alternative. Adonis remains for me a major formal and historical achievement, and I am keeping him as an alternative because the question about the later collections is still unanswered, not because it has been answered against him. This rests on public knowledge of the works. I have not independently re-read or verified any text.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation about Cărtărescu is the one his supporters name. The effect lives in long, rhythmically dense Romanian sentences, and translation may flatten or alter the voice I am praising. The encyclopedic, self-reflexive mode may deepen across the largest novels, or it may harden into repetition of motifs. I cannot settle that without close reading of Solenoid and the later volumes by readers of Romanian. His poetry and essays are thinly covered in translation, so a whole-oeuvre claim is partial and the citation should not overstate it. There is also a reservation about my own movement. Adonis's case may be weaker in this exchange because it depends on a language none of us can assess, not because the work is weaker. If the Academy's expert input on Arabic poetry were to establish the continuing force and sustained quality of the later collections, I would reconsider. I accept that my preference for a candidate whose case is easier to argue from structure could favour writers who translate more readily.

responses.point: Mattson puts Cărtărescu first and argues that the large-scale architecture of his prose survives translation better than prosodic mastery does. She would frame the citation around the prose cycles with the poetry as foundation. She also treats wider translation as supporting context only and not as evidence of quality.
responses.response: I agree with your framing of the citation and with your point that wider translation is not evidence of quality. I still do not claim that the architecture survives translation intact. Your argument that it survives better than prosody is the reason I moved. In round 1 I said translation loss runs in both directions and is not a reason to rank one candidate above another. I still think so. What changed is that you and Sem-Sandberg gave a difference in kind, and I cannot answer that difference with evidence from the later Arabic poems. Your open question about density as depth or excess is also mine. Without close reading of the Romanian, I can only treat the coherence of the project, from the poetry through the Blinding cycle to Solenoid, as the evidence we have. I cannot treat it as proof.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second. He argues that translation loss differs in kind for the two writers and that Adonis's later work raises the same open question as Cărtărescu's. He also warns against counting age, essays or public positions as literary merit.
responses.response: Your point about the difference in kind is the one I could not rebut, and it is part of why I have moved. I keep my objection to letting that difference decide by itself, and I am glad you do not use it that way. On your last point I agree completely. Age, essays and public positions are not merit, and I will not let timing carry Adonis. Your question whether the late novels' intensity is sustained or merely maintained deserves to be put to the committee as a question about the texts. I would add that the same question stands for Adonis's later collections, and neither of us can settle it from the supplied evidence. That is why he stays on my list of alternatives.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first. She argues that scholarship and poetry become one practice in Carson's work and that the citation should not rest on the novelty of hybridity alone. She also says that if the committee's standard is mainly large-scale sustained architecture, Cărtărescu fits it more naturally than Carson does, and that the will does not require that standard.
responses.response: Your last point is the strongest challenge to my new position, and I take it seriously. A preference for architectural scale is a standard the committee should choose openly and not adopt by default. I do not hold that scale is the only measure of a whole oeuvre, and my movement toward Cărtărescu is not a claim that formal renewal across genres counts for less. I keep Carson as a strong alternative because her voice and formal intelligence are distinctive, and the question of her design-dependent works is a caution about method and not about quality. On translations and scholarship, I agree with you that they belong to the context and ground of the original writing, not to separate claims in a citation. I also still doubt that her compact, partly object-based corpus can be compared with a large prose project on volume alone, and I do not think you ask that. My difference with you is a close judgment about cumulative formal achievement, and I hold it provisionally.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She says the citation for Carson should rest on the poems and formal intelligence of the core books, with translations as context. She also says she cannot build a preference on Adonis's case because she cannot assess it directly, and that this gap is not a point against him.
responses.response: I accept your distinction between a limit in what a member can assess and a point against a writer. It is the reason I did not move Adonis down from limited respect for the poems. I moved because I cannot argue his later output to you from the work itself. Your core-books approach for Carson is the right discipline for any hybrid oeuvre, and it is the standard I would also apply to a Cărtărescu citation. The citation rests on the prose project, the poetry is named as its foundation, and it does not claim an assessment of the whole corpus that we cannot make. I also note that your second place for Cărtărescu rests on a case you rate as strong, and that this is the main reason I consider the B029 and B012 positions close.

uncertainties: Whether Solenoid and the later novels deepen the earlier architecture or re-run its obsessions cannot be settled without close reading by readers of Romanian, and I have not read or independently verified any text for this stage.

How far Cărtărescu's rhythmically dense Romanian prose survives translation is uncertain, and his poetry and essays are thinly covered, so the citation scope should stay on the prose project with the poetry as foundation.

Whether the later Adonis collections sustain the level of the early and middle work, and whether the Academy's regional expert input on Arabic poetry can establish this, remains the unanswered question behind my move.

Whether preferring architectural scale over formal renewal across genres is a standard the will requires or one I am adopting by default is unresolved, and I cannot settle the reading of the will's phrase about an idealistic direction from the supplied evidence.

How to weigh Carson's design-dependent, hybrid works and her translation and scholarship against a large prose project under common criteria, and Tawada's Japanese and German corpus given uneven translation coverage, remains open.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1: none apparent from the supplied profile. As chair I disclose that my round 1 first choice was Adonis and that my first choice has now changed to Cărtărescu for the reasons above. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and Celan's late work is intellectual context only and is not evidence of a preference for any candidate. No personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted writer appears in the profile. The Academy's ceremony speeches I have given are presented on behalf of the Academy and do not establish a personal vote. This note reports only what the profile and the round 1 files state and is not independently verified.
